items.readable_text:
Content:
Rationalizing the denominator works similarly for algebraic expressions as it does for numerical ones. When the denominator contains two terms and includes radicals, we multiply both the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator to eliminate the radical.

Content:
For example, consider the following expression:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{x}}]

Content:
To find the conjugate of the denominator [MATH: 1+\sqrt{x},] all we have to do is flip the sign between the two terms. So, the conjugate of the denominator is

Content:
[MATH: 1\,{\color{blue}{-}}\,\sqrt{x}.]

Content:
Now, to rationalize the denominator, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by [MATH: 1-\sqrt{x}] and simplify:

Content:
[MATH: (1)/(1 + sqrt(x))|=; (1)/(1 + sqrt(x)) ⋅ (1 − sqrt(x))/(1 − sqrt(x))|=; (1 − sqrt(x))/((1 + sqrt(x))(1 − sqrt(x)))|=; (1 − sqrt(x))/(1^{2} − (sqrt(x))^{2})|=; (1 − sqrt(x))/(1 − x)]

items.title: Rationalizing Denominators Containing Two Terms

sections.normalized_html:
First, note that the denominator's conjugate is [MATH: 3+\sqrt a.]

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate [MATH: 3+\sqrt a,] and simplify:

[MATH: (1)/(3 − sqrt(a))|=; (1)/(3 − sqrt(a)) ⋅ (3 + sqrt(a))/(3 + sqrt(a))|=; (3 + sqrt(a))/((3 − sqrt(a))(3 + sqrt(a)))|=; (3 + sqrt(a))/(3^{2} − (sqrt(a))^{2})|=; (3 + sqrt(a))/(9 − a)]

Example Prompt:
Rationalize the denominator of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{3-\sqrt a}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, note that the denominator's conjugate is [MATH: 3+\sqrt a.]

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate [MATH: 3+\sqrt a,] and simplify:

[MATH: (1)/(3 − sqrt(a))|=; (1)/(3 − sqrt(a)) ⋅ (3 + sqrt(a))/(3 + sqrt(a))|=; (3 + sqrt(a))/((3 − sqrt(a))(3 + sqrt(a)))|=; (3 + sqrt(a))/(3^{2} − (sqrt(a))^{2})|=; (3 + sqrt(a))/(9 − a)]

items.title: Rationalizing Denominators Containing a Binomial Within the Radical

sections.normalized_html:
First, note that the denominator's conjugate is [MATH: \sqrt{x+1}-1.]

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate [MATH: \sqrt{x+1}-1,] and simplify:

[MATH: \eqalign{ \dfrac {x} {\sqrt{x+1}+1} &= \[5pt] \dfrac {x} {\sqrt{x+1}+1}\cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{x+1}-1}{\sqrt{x+1}-1} &= \[5pt] \dfrac {x(\sqrt{x+1}-1)} {(\sqrt{x+1}+1)(\sqrt{x+1}-1)} &= \[5pt] \dfrac {x(\sqrt{x+1}-1)} {(\sqrt{x+1})^2-1^2} &= \[5pt] \dfrac {x(\sqrt{x+1}-1)} {x+1-1} &= \[5pt] \dfrac {x(\sqrt{x+1}-1)} {x}&=\[5pt] \sqrt{x+1}-1 }]

items.title: Rationalizing a Denominator With Two Radicals

sections.normalized_html:
First, note that the denominator's conjugate is [MATH: \sqrt{2}+\sqrt{x}.]

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate [MATH: \sqrt{2}+\sqrt{x},] and simplify:

[MATH: \eqalign{ \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{x}} &= \[5pt] \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{x}} \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{x}} &= \[5pt] \dfrac{x(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{x}) }{(\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{x})(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{x})} &= \[5pt] \dfrac{x(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{x}) }{(\sqrt{2})^2-(\sqrt{x})^2} &= \[5pt] \dfrac{x(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{x}) }{2-x} }]

Item 5 — Example: Rationalizing Denominators Containing a Binomial Within the Radical

Example Prompt:
Rationalize the denominator of [MATH: \dfrac {x} {\sqrt{x+1}+1}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, note that the denominator's conjugate is [MATH: \sqrt{x+1}-1.]

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate [MATH: \sqrt{x+1}-1,] and simplify:

[MATH: \eqalign{
\dfrac {x} {\sqrt{x+1}+1} &= \[5pt]
\dfrac {x} {\sqrt{x+1}+1}\cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{x+1}-1}{\sqrt{x+1}-1} &= \[5pt]
\dfrac {x(\sqrt{x+1}-1)} {(\sqrt{x+1}+1)(\sqrt{x+1}-1)} &= \[5pt]
\dfrac {x(\sqrt{x+1}-1)} {(\sqrt{x+1})^2-1^2} &= \[5pt]
\dfrac {x(\sqrt{x+1}-1)} {x+1-1} &= \[5pt]
\dfrac {x(\sqrt{x+1}-1)} {x}&=\[5pt]
\sqrt{x+1}-1
}]

\dfrac{x(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{x}) }{2-x}
}]
